report.headline: Already below-average usage in the EuroLeague projects to fall further in the NBA, with an efficiency forecast that carries no real signal

projection.text: The model projects a 12.6% NBA usage rate, down from 15.6% in the EuroLeague, roughly 1.4 standard deviations below the NBA's minutes-weighted average of 20.1% (sd 5.4%).

risks.text: His EuroLeague usage rate stood 0.97 standard deviations below his league's average and his true-shooting percentage 0.45 standard deviations below average, whereas the historical cohort of EL->NBA movers this model is built on averaged +0.46 standard deviations above their league — making this a less typical mover than most in the training data.
The source season rests on only 934 minutes across 36 games at age 27, a thin base for projecting either usage or efficiency forward.

The usage rate projection sits well below the NBA average with a 95% interval (4.3%-20.9%) spanning nearly the entire observed range of NBA usage rates, so a marginal-role outcome cannot be distinguished from a below-replacement one.

No trustworthy efficiency projection exists here: the true-shooting model loses to the naive league-mean baseline (4.7% MAE for both), so any stated true-shooting number should not be treated as a forecast.

strengths.text: Turned the ball over at a modest 13.3% rate while posting a 9.7% assist rate and 2.235 assists per 75 possessions, suggesting efficient decision-making within a limited playmaking role.
Rebounded at 5.625 per 75 possessions despite a low 15.6% usage rate, indicating activity on the glass beyond his shot-creation role.
Took 44.9% of his shot attempts from three, a profile that fits a floor-spacing, low-usage role of the kind that translates most directly across leagues.
On usage rate specifically, the model beats the best trivial baseline (3.3% MAE vs 4.3%), so the projected decline in role is at least a metric where the model has demonstrated some predictive value.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate runs from 7.1% to 18.0%, a span of nearly 11 points — about two standard deviations of the league's usage distribution — so the model can flag this as a low-usage profile but cannot pin down where in that range he lands; the 95% interval (4.3%-20.9%) covers almost the league's full spread. The true-shooting projection (53.5%, 80% interval 46.8%-60.2%) should not be read as informative: the model's error on this metric (4.7% MAE) is no better than simply guessing the league average (4.7%), so it adds nothing beyond that baseline.
